title: Move-Then-Operate: Behavioral Phasing for Robotic Manipulation
one_liner: Split robotic manipulation into two separate experts—one for reaching, one for touching—so the robot learns each skill without interference.
lead: Humans manipulate objects by doing two very different things in sequence: first, we move our hand to the right spot (coarse motion), then we adjust grip and contact to interact with the object (fine motion). Traditional robot-learning systems force a single neural network to do both, which confuses learning. This paper adds an automatic gatekeeper that picks which expert handles each moment, so each expert becomes world-class at its job.

problem.h2: Monolithic policies conflate two very different jobs
paras: A robot grasping a coffee mug must do two physically distinct things: (1) move its arm across the table to reach the mug (coarse, long-range motion), then (2) fine-tune grip pressure and wrist angle to lift without spilling (precise contact). A naive single neural network tries to learn both rules at once.

The problem: reaching and grasping have opposite dynamics. Reaching is about trajectory smoothness and obstacle avoidance; grasping is about instantaneous force and tactile feedback. When the network trains on both, gradients for reaching goals (move my arm faster) collide with gradients for contact goals (reduce grip force) because both flow backward through the same set of weights. For example, increasing the speed of arm motion requires larger weight changes, but increasing grip sensitivity requires the opposite weight adjustments—when the network tries to update a weight to satisfy one goal, it moves away from the other goal. The network learns a muddy compromise neither job is good at. A robot that reaches well accidentally squashes fragile objects. One that grasps well is too cautious and overshoots the target.

Why a beginner's fix fails: you might try training two separate networks, but then you need a human to label when the robot should switch from one to the other—tedious, and the switch points won't match how the robot actually moves.

callout.html: Add a learned phase-selector gate that automatically picks which expert to run at each moment, with labels generated by an AI system that watches where the end-effector is moving.

steps.text: Feed training videos into a large vision-language model with prompts about end-effector velocity. It marks each frame 'reaching' or 'grasping'.
One learns only reaching trajectories; one learns only grasping. Each gradient points cleanly toward its job.
A small network watches the current scene and outputs scores for each phase. A loss function teaches it to match the labels.
When the robot acts, the router looks at the scene once and picks the expert with the highest score. That expert generates the arm commands.
Unlike routers that decide once per visual word, this one decides once per timestep, keeping the expert choice stable across the generated action sequence.

object.h2: What the paper changes: the policy architecture
paras: Instead of one monolithic network that outputs actions, the paper builds two expert networks (one for reaching, one for grasping) and adds a learned gate that picks which expert runs at each moment. The gate watches the scene and outputs scores that favor either reaching or grasping.

hidden.name: phase label correctness
paras: The paper introduces a quantity that was previously invisible: which moments in a manipulation sequence belong to reaching versus grasping. This matters because if the labels are wrong, an expert trained on mislabeled data learns a confused skill.

The paper estimates this by feeding demonstration videos into a large vision-language model (an AI that understands both images and language) with a carefully written prompt. The prompt includes clues like end-effector velocity, subtask boundaries, and human-motor heuristics. The AI labels each frame, and those labels seed training. Correct labels concentrate each expert's learning on one job; wrong labels bleed interference back in.

heat.caption: Brighter means network receives clearer reaching-vs-grasping signal. Mistakes (mislabeled transitions) darken that cell.

reads.html: The paper's invisible lever is automatic labeling. A smart system watches videos and says 'reaching now, grasping now.' That separation is what makes training clean.

The phase labels are generated by an MLLM-based pipeline conditioned on end-effector velocity, subtask decomposition, and human motor pattern heuristics. Router training minimizes a loss function (how wrong the prediction is) against these labels.

paras: In a monolithic network, the gradient for 'move faster' and the gradient for 'reduce grip force' both flow backward through the same weights, creating a tug-of-war. Moving faster gets blocked because the network learned to focus carefully on grip safety.

Here, reaching gradients flow only through the reaching expert, and grasping gradients only through the grasping expert. No collision, no compromise. Each expert's weights receive clean signals about what that phase needs. The reaching expert learns to focus on trajectory smoothness without worrying about force. The grasping expert learns precise force without trying to solve navigation. At runtime, the router simply picks the right expert—because the router watches velocity and other cues that correlate with the true phase, it naturally picks the expert whose training is most relevant to what the robot needs to do right now.

stages.s: Observation: arm position, object location, force sensor
Router pools visual features, outputs phase probability
Pick expert (reaching or grasping) via greedy decode
Selected expert attends to shared features

math.h2: The routing loss: teaching the gate
math.words: Cross-entropy between predicted phase and ground-truth phase label, computed from pooled visual features.
symbols: pooled visual feature at timestep t (what does the scene look like now)
small neural network that reads the pooled feature
turn raw scores into probabilities that add to 1
ground-truth phase label: 1 if reaching, 0 if grasping
cross-entropy (how wrong is our prediction compared to truth)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: At timestep t=3, the robot is reaching (y_t is reaching).
Router reads the scene features and outputs raw scores [0.8, 0.2] for [reaching, grasping].
Normalize scores to fractions summing to 1: [0.73, 0.27].
Loss = -log(0.73) = 0.31 (low penalty because prediction was mostly right).
At timestep t=5, the robot is grasping (y_t is grasping), but router outputs [0.5, 0.5].
Loss = -log(0.5) = 0.69 (higher penalty; the router was confused).
During training, gradients nudge the MLP to predict more confidently when it sees reaching-like or grasping-like features.

math.note: The router is trained separately from the experts, using only the phase labels, so it learns to predict 'what phase are we in' from the scene.

items.html: If the vision-language model incorrectly labels the transition from reaching to grasping, an expert trains on mixed signals. For instance, if it labels the moment the hand touches the mug as still reaching, the reaching expert learns a tiny twitch that confuses later grasping.

The router learns from end-effector velocity and scene features. If lighting or camera angle correlates with phase in the training set but not in deployment, the router misclassifies. A dimly lit reaching action gets routed to the grasping expert.

Both experts use the same vision-language encoder. If reaching and grasping require different visual features (one cares about distance to target, the other about contact pressure), the shared encoder may not represent both well.

Automatic labeling via MLLM with velocity cues produces clean phase boundaries. Router trains on a large pool of diverse trajectories so it generalizes. Experts have enough capacity to learn specialized skills. Performance plateaus at 84% average success, well above the monolithic 58%.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal simulation (e.g., PyBullet or MuJoCo) where a robot arm must reach and grasp three different objects (a mug, a bottle, a small block). Train a monolithic baseline on 100 trajectories. Train Move-Then-Operate on the same 100 trajectories, using automatic MLLM labels. Measure success as: (1) did the robot reach the target without hitting obstacles, and (2) did it maintain stable grip without dropping.
demo.closing: The demo proves that two experts with a learned gate outperform one muddled network on the same data budget because each expert's weights receive focused training signals pointing in one direction, whereas the monolithic network's weights receive conflicting signals that cancel each other out.
